fieldFixes.summary: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin showed that the Netflix Prize dataset of movie ratings by 500,000 subscribers, released with names removed, could be de-anonymised: with 8 ratings (two of which could be wrong) and dates within 14 days, 99% of records could be uniquely identified. Using public IMDb ratings from a small sample of about 50 IMDb users as background knowledge, they identified known users' Netflix records, revealing apparent political preferences. A first version appeared on arXiv on 18 October 2006, and the IMDb identifications were reported in the revision of 22 November 2007. The paper was presented at the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, held at the Claremont Resort in Oakland on 18–21 May 2008.

issues: The significance overstates: 'The first person-side machine-readable privacy signal on the web.' The record's own source says ad-network opt-out cookies had existed 'For more than a decade', 'through which consumers could signal to the companies' their choice. It also says a header had been proposed months earlier: Dan Kaminsky suggested an 'X-No-Track' header, and in March 2009 Mozilla's Mike Shaver asked 'Could we not just standardize/promote a header like X-Tracking-Opt-Out'. The Soghoian–Stamm add-on was an early implemented prototype of the header, not the first signal.

The summary said the idea 'replaced dozens of per-network opt-out cookies'. It replaced nothing. Soghoian pitched it in mid-July 2009 and 'none of the advertising firms showed any interest in the header', and he 'ultimately decided against including the header in TACO'. 'Dozens' also understates: TACO 'eventually grew to include more than 100 different opt out cookies'.

fieldFixes.summary: In July 2009 privacy researcher Christopher Soghoian, with his research collaborator Sid Stamm, built a prototype Firefox add-on that added two headers to outgoing web requests: 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1' and 'X-Do-Not-Track: 1'. It was meant to replace per-company opt-out cookies with one signal sent to every server; Soghoian's own TACO add-on had grown to more than 100 of them. Dan Kaminsky and Mozilla's Mike Shaver had urged the header approach earlier that year. When Soghoian pitched it to industry in mid-July 2009, none of the advertising firms showed any interest, and he never added it to TACO.
fieldFixes.significance: The seed of the browser's Do Not Track header: the person's browser would send one machine-readable preference to every server, instead of the person collecting an opt-out from each company. But it was only a yes/no request with no legal force, and advertisers were free to ignore it.

issues: 'The next day' is wrong. The Register article was published 2012-02-20T22:26:45Z. Cubrilovic's post has published_time 'Tue Feb 21 2012 15:40:52 GMT+1100', which is 04:40 UTC on 21 February, still the evening of 20 February in the US. It opens 'There is a post today on a Microsoft MSDN blog'. His post came within hours of Microsoft's, not the next day.

The Cranor claim is overstated. Her words are 'no regulators have announced that they are investigating any website for a deceptive P3P policy', which is not the same as 'no regulator had acted'. Her post is dated 3 December 2012.

Mechanism wording: IE did not 'treat as valid' a policy reading 'This is not a P3P policy!'. The Register explains that 'if the code is not recognized, Internet Explorer will accept it anyway', and Cubrilovic says IE by default accepts third-party cookies with 'a header that doesn't state policy'. Google's reply is quoted more exactly: it was 'impractical to comply with Microsoft’s request while providing modern web functionality'.

The original IEBlog post (blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/ie/2012/02/20/google-bypassing-user-privacy-settings/) now redirects to a learn.microsoft.com archive URL that returns an authorization or index page, so it could not be read directly. Hachamovitch's post of 20 February 2012 is corroborated by The Register and by Cubrilovic.

fieldFixes.summary: On 20 February 2012 Dean Hachamovitch, Microsoft's vice-president for Internet Explorer, wrote that Google was circumventing IE's default privacy protection by sending a P3P compact policy reading 'This is not a P3P policy!'. Because IE accepts a compact policy whose tokens it does not recognise, Google's third-party cookies got through. Google replied that it was 'impractical to comply with Microsoft's request while providing modern web functionality'. Within hours, researcher Nik Cubrilovic showed that Facebook sent a similar non-policy ('Facebook does not have a P3P policy'). In December 2012 Lorrie Cranor, who had spent seven years working on the P3P 1.0 specification, noted that no regulator had announced an investigation of any website for a deceptive P3P policy.
